display_title: Interesting idea but clarifications are needed

content.title: Interesting idea but clarifications are needed
content.review:
This paper proposes a video prediction method called Neural Uncertainty Priors. The method is based on CVAE and the key idea is to weigh the MSE loss by an uncertainty estimate of the generated sample so that uncertain frames have less contribution to the loss. The uncertainty estimate is produced by learning a mapping from the learned latent prior’s covariance to the variance of the decoder normal distribution inside a variational inference framework. An adversarial sequence discriminator is also used to encourage realistic video generation. Experiments are conducted on three public datasets and show superior performance and faster convergence than SOTA approaches especially for small amount of data.


**Pros:**

++ The paper is clearly written, well-motivated and easy to understand  
++ The idea of connecting the variance of the prior to the variance of the decoder distribution is interesting, and the paper has proposed a sensible way of doing it  
++ The experiments and ablation studies are extensive and have demonstrated the proposed method outperforms prior work  

**Concerns:**

-- I feel an important baseline is missing, i.e., outputting the variance of the decoder normal distribution by the VAE decoder, which is a standard way of calibrating the decoder (e.g., [4]).  
-- Could the authors elaborate on how the hyperpriors are chosen based on problem-specific knowledge?  
-- In Fig. 2, the performance of other methods (e.g., Hsieh et al) seems to be still increasing. Have they really converged at 100 epochs? Are there plots for more epochs? Also, I would recommend evaluating the performance more densely along the epochs. Right now, it seems like only the performance of epoch 1, 5, 100 has been evaluated.  
-- How is the subset of training samples (e.g. 600 samples) selected in Table 1? Has any cross-validation been done to make sure the model outperforms on average?  
-- The diversity metric used in the paper in Fig 2 is a bit strange to me. Higher SSIM doesn’t necessarily mean better diversity. And other methods show a larger increase in SSIM with the same number of additional samples, which seems to indicate that those methods have better sample diversity.  
-- Sequence discriminator is not really novel. It has been extensively used in trajectory prediction, motion prediction[3], as well as video prediction [1,2].  
-- Since it is video generation, some video results would help us judge the quality of the generated videos better.  

[1] Predicting Future Frames using Retrospective Cycle GAN. Kwon et al. CVPR 2019.  
[2] Dual Motion GAN for Future-Flow Embedded Video Prediction. Liang et al. ICCV 2017.  
[3] HP-GAN: Probabilistic 3D human motion prediction via GAN. Barsoum et al. CVPRW 2018.  
[4] Simple and Effective VAE Training with Calibrated Decoders. 2020.  


**Rating Justification:**

I like the overall idea of this paper, which is to connect the variance of the prior to the decoder distribution. However, I do have a few questions and concerns about the experiments. I’m leaning slightly towards accept for now.


**Additional Comments:**

Sec 3. Right before Eq 1, “log-partition function”, shouldn’t it be just partition function?  
Sec 5. “Sequences that matches“ -> “match”

content.title: Review
content.review:
Summary:
This paper proposes a method for future frame prediction that models the uncertainty in the latent space directly in the frame space. The proposed method allows for penalizing pixels with more uncertainty less than the pixels with high uncertainty. In addition, a sequence discriminator is proposed which makes sure the generated frames stay within the data distribution. In their experiments, they outperform the baselines. They also show that the proposed method speeds up learning.


Pros:
+ New approach for video prediction that transfers uncertainty from latent space to pixel space directly for training speed
+ Outperforms baselines


Comments / Questions:

- Comparison with method without discriminator
In Table1, the authors provide comparisons with the baselines only against their full method. If I am not mistaken, the main contribution of this paper is about handling uncertainty and the discriminator is the cherry on top. Therefore, in terms of probabilistic models, there should be a row without discriminator in Table1. Otherwise, we cannot tell whether it’s the discriminator that causes the improvement.

- Using the discriminator on the baselines
In addition to the previous comment, there should be an experiment where the baselines are trained with the discriminator for fair comparison. This way we can be sure that the new uncertainty model plays an important role in the frame prediction.

- Evaluation metrics:
By now, everyone doing video prediction are aware that PSNR and SSIM alone are not good metrics for video prediction. Therefore, evaluation metrics such as LPIPS, FID, FVD, or even user studies are usually included as part of the evaluation. At least, the first three mentioned should be provided in the rebuttal to help reviewers make a more informed decision about the performance of this method since the main message is about having a more accurate prediction due to the uncertainty handling.


Conclusion:
I would like to see the items mentioned above before coming to a final conclusion about this paper. For now, I feel the submission is below the acceptance line.
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

content.title: Official Review #4
content.review:
The main idea of this paper is to weight the reconstruction loss of a visual predictive model by an estimate of its uncertainty. The paper experiments on the BAIR Push dataset and the KTH Activity Recognition dataset.

Strengths:
The underlying idea of this paper is interesting. Instead of learning a predictive model with a reconstruction loss or just an adversarial loss, the paper introduces a model that estimates its own uncertainty in the future, and uses this uncertainty estimate to predict which features/pixels should be predicted in the future. 

Since there is significant amount of interest in predictive models today, this paper could have a strong impact on the community. 

The authors compare against reasonable baselines (although see below about limited experimental gains).

Weaknesses:
The experimental results are fairly limited. The evaluated datasets are fairly simple, and the gains over the previous state-of-the-art is minor (less than half a point). It is not clear that the complexity of the method is justified for the performance gains.

The chosen evaluation metrics are likely not suitable for this task. PSNR will be very similar to MSE -- in such cases, we should not expect the method to outperform an MSE model under this metric. The experiments would be much stronger if they directly evaluated the key advantages of the proposed idea. Does the model actually figure out which parts of the video are predictable or not? Can you visualize what regions of the video are predictable or not? Does the model generate more diverse outputs? 

The paper is fairly difficult to read. There are many grammar and spelling mistakes, and the order of presentation could be clarified. The paper makes also several claims that are inaccurate. These are minor points, but they should be fixed before publication:
- The abstract undersells prior work by suggesting the work relies on MSE. Most serious video generation models do not use MSE. 
- The first sentence requires a citation "extrapolating the present into the future is a task humans do effortlessly" and should be at least qualified. People cannot predict everything effortlessly, as this sentence implies. 

I think this could have been a strong paper. With additional experiments that focus on the main idea and cleaning up the writing, it can be a great paper.

display_title: Review for Learning to Generate Videos Using Neural Uncertainty Priors

content.title: Review for Learning to Generate Videos Using Neural Uncertainty Priors
content.review:
#########################
SUMMARY

The authors propose a modified training objective for VAE-based video prediction models. In particular, the goal of this formulation is to not penalize predictions that might be plausible but deviate from the given ground truth future sequence during training, which the authors identify as an issue with previous approaches. This is mainly achieved by weighting the reconstruction loss part of the ELBO based on the variance of the prior latent distribution and introducing new terms to the ELBO objective. Experimental results indicate that this objective might outperform previous approaches.

#########################
STRENGTHS AND WEAKNESSES

[+] Encouraging empirical results 
[-] The motivation for the approach is not well-supported - during training we sample from the posterior, so there is no uncertainty as to what is the ground truth future.
[-] The novel loss is not well motivated from a variational inference point of view, contrary to what the authors state - there is no proper ELBO derivation and the adversarial loss is not well justified
[-] Overall the paper lacks rigor

#########################
DETAILED COMMENTS

The main issue with the paper is its motivation. The authors seek a way of weighting the loss associated to high uncertainty frames (because the future is not deterministic, and certain frames might depict more plausible future outcomes than others) so as to not penalize the model for making a plausible but incorrect prediction with respect to a given ground truth. However, VAE-based models are trained by sampling from the approximate posterior, meaning that the reconstruction loss is computed for a frame sampled when we have access to the future outcome. Therefore, uncertainty might play a role in having a large KL-divergence between the prior and the posterior distribution, but the reconstruction loss will not unnecessarily penalize highly uncertain frames because that uncertainty can be resolved through the posterior.

Furthermore, the proposed modified objective is not properly supported from a variational inference point of view. The adversarial loss is added without proper justification, while it is unclear why the rest of the terms are introduced. I would suggest that the authors provide a proper graphical model for their approach and perform a step-by-step derivation of the ELBO. In its current form, the final objective seems like a convoluted way of weighting the reconstruction loss based on the variance of the prior. Not having a proper variational inference justification would not be in itself an issue, however given the author claims and the motivation for the approach this becomes an important point.

Finally, the paper lacks rigor in many of the claims and in its experimental setup. In its introduction, the authors should support some of the statements with references (such as "humans extrapolate the future effortlessly"). In section 3, the authors state that equation 1 with the reparametrization trick "boils down to an MSE objective", which is inaccurate as it is a MSE loss for the reconstruction part with a very particular regularization, and only if using an isotropic gaussian observation model. Similar vague statements are found throughout section 3 and 4. For the experimental section, many details are missing such as what is the actual architecture used to implement the proposed approach (layers, networks, size of the layers, optimizer, etc.) and the details on how some of the baselines were implemented/trained/evaluated.

#########################
SCORE
I vote for rejecting this paper. The novel objective is not well justified both from a motivation point of view and from variational inference perspective. The empirical results are currently the strongest argument for the paper, but there are issues with the experimental setup. Ultimately, even if the results are encouraging, it is not clear why this approach is sound and why it would be better than other VAE models.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
